title: Botanical fern frond in cross-stitch
subtitle: A single fern frond in five greens on 14-count Aida
excerpt: A botanical fern frond is a 45-by-100 stitch piece on 14-count Aida. A single arching frond with its alternating pinnae is stitched in five greens. The narrow composition finishes at about 8 x 18 cm and suits a tall slim frame. No back-stitch is needed, the pinnae shapes are distinct enough in full crosses.
sourceNotes: Original design for Homemade cross-stitch library. Botanical fern illustration conventions follow Sowerby's English Botany (1790-1814), scanned by the British Library and available on Archive.org.

content.text: A botanical fern frond is a 45-by-100 stitch piece on 14-count
. Five greens describe the arching rachis (central rib) and the alternating pinnae (leaflets) that fan out from it. The

colour progression goes from darkest green at the base rachis to the palest yellow-green at the outer pinna tips. The finished piece is about 8 x 18 cm and all stitches are full crosses, no back-stitch is needed.

items.name: 14-count Aida, white or cream
items.substitutions: Very pale sage Aida blends gently with the greens

items.name: Frame or hoop
items.qty: Slim portrait frame or narrow hoop frame

content.text: Find the centre of the fabric. The chart centre falls roughly at the midpoint of the frond, on the rachis. Begin there with 3346 (mid dark green) on the central rib and work outward along the rib toward the tip and base.

Stitch each pinna from the rachis outward. The innermost stitches of each pinna are darker (3346, 3347); the outer tips are in the lighter greens (3348, 471). Work each pinna pair before moving to the next.

The base of the rachis is in the darkest green (3345) and narrows to a single-stitch column before the first pinna. The tip of the frond curls very slightly, follow the chart exactly here, as the curve is represented by a stepped offset of one stitch every three rows.
Wash gently and press face-down. A slim portrait frame, unmatted, with a pale green or off-white surround suits the botanical style.

items.symptom: The pinnae (leaflets) are uneven in size
items.cause: Each leaflet was stitched freehand rather than following the counted outline on the chart.
items.fix: Count the chart squares for each leaflet before starting: each pinnule should be the same number of squares wide. Work from the central rib outward on each side. Once the rib stitches are in, the leaflets should be symmetrical.

items.symptom: The frond looks too light in the leaf areas
items.cause: Only two strands were used where the chart calls for three, or the thread was not stripped before stitching.
items.fix: Strip two strands from the skein and recombine. On 14-count the stitches should cover the Aida squares fully when the strands are correctly stripped. Work a single test stitch and check coverage before continuing the frond fill.

content.text: A matched pair of fern fronds mirrored left-to-right makes a striking symmetric display. For more colour variety, the poppy-and-seed-head or daffodil-sprig patterns in this sub-category use the same narrow vertical format.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.
